---
title: "Retinal vessels: tiling, and a metric Dice cannot replace"
description: "A 2048-pixel photograph cut into tiles, scored on connectedness, and the two choices in the configuration that were measured afterwards."
mirrors: retinal-vessels
---

[FIVES](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.19688169.v1) is 800 colour fundus photographs at
2048 x 2048 - 200 each of normal, AMD, diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma - with a vessel
tree drawn over every one. It is CC BY 4.0, it ships its own balanced train/test split, and
it is the only dataset in this documentation that cannot be handed to a network whole.

Three things here appear in no other article, and each is the reason this dataset was chosen.

**It tiles.** `splits` reads each image at full resolution and cuts it into a grid of inputs.

**It is scored on a metric Dice cannot stand in for.** clDice asks whether a structure is
*connected* rather than whether its pixels coincide, and a skeleton is a property of a whole
mask, so it is measured on the reassembled image rather than on the tiles.

**It reports per disease rather than as one mean**, which is how the interesting thing about
this dataset was found - and the interesting thing turns out not to be about the disease.

**Where the numbers come from.** Everything below is one run of
`examples/segment_retinal_vessels.py` at its own defaults - 40 epochs, 6.7 hours on a GTX
1070 - whose record is `measurements/fives/fives.json` in the project's workbench, with the
quality join printed by `measurements/fives/quality.py` and the figure drawn by that same
script's `--figures`. Unlike the other articles' figures, this one cannot be redrawn from
published weights alone: it is this run's prediction, and the script draws it at the end of
the run rather than from a file. The published `fives-unet` weights
are a **second** run of exactly this configuration and score 0.8789 where this one scores
0.8828; where a number below belongs to those weights rather than to this run, it says so.
The last section is different again and says so in its own first paragraph.

This page mirrors `vignette("retinal-vessels")` in the R package, which is the source for the
prose: the walk is the same, the route is not. R reaches these destinations through
constructors; here they are reached through a configuration file.

## Why a vessel cannot be resized

FIVES images are 2048 x 2048, and the obvious move is to resize them to something a U-Net is
comfortable with. It is the wrong move here, and the reason is a measurement rather than a
preference.

A FIVES vessel is **about nine pixels wide** - measured as mask area over skeleton length,
over six random masks. Resized to 256 the same vessels are about 1.2 pixels. That matters
because of what happens at one pixel: shift a one-pixel structure by a single pixel and it
overlaps the truth *nowhere at all*, so Dice, IoU and clDice alike read zero and none of them
can tell a near miss from a total failure. Tiling keeps the data out of that regime, which is
what `splits` is for.

(The nine-pixel figure corrects the one-to-five this dataset is usually described with. One to
five is what remains after a resize - a property of the preprocessing, not of the retina.)

The last section of this page measures what that claim is actually worth, and it is narrower
than this paragraph makes it sound.

## The data

One 1.7 GB download, CC BY 4.0. The authors' own split is already balanced across the four
groups - 150 train and 50 test of each - so it is used rather than replaced.

The archive is laid out as `Original/` and `Ground truth/` with matching file names, which is
not a layout the package discovers on its own, so the pairs are written into a CSV and the
specification reads that:

```python
from pathlib import Path

FOLDER = "FIVES A Fundus Image Dataset for AI-based Vessel Segmentation"

def write_split(root: Path, split: str, out: Path) -> int:
    # `glob("*.png")` rather than everything in the directory: the archive ships a
    # `Thumbs.db` beside the 600 training images, and a Windows thumbnail cache is not a
    # fundus photograph. Filtering by extension is also what keeps the pairing below honest.
    images = sorted((root / FOLDER / split / "Original").glob("*.png"))
    rows = ["key,images,masks"]
    for image in images:
        mask = root / FOLDER / split / "Ground truth" / image.name
        if not mask.exists():
            raise SystemExit(f"{image.name} has no mask beside it")
        # The key is the file's own name. Without it a `config_file` sample is called
        # `row 55`, which names nothing on disk and cannot be grouped by - and grouping is
        # most of what this page has to say.
        rows.append(f"{image.stem},{image.resolve()},{mask.resolve()}")
    out.write_text("\n".join(rows) + "\n")
    return len(images)
```

The disease is in the file name - `_N`, `_A`, `_D`, `_G` for normal, AMD, diabetic retinopathy
and glaucoma - which is what the grouping below reads.

## The configuration

```yaml
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: measurements/fives/splits/train.csv
  validation_path: measurements/fives/splits/test.csv
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
  mode: config_file
models:
  - name: vessels
    architecture: u_net
    input_shape: [512, 512]
    # 2048 read whole and cut 4 x 4. This is the field the page exists for.
    splits: [4, 4]
    blocks: 4
    filters: 16
    batch_size: 4
    epochs: 40
    loss:
      name: cce_dice
    metrics:
      - name: dice
        include_background: false
      - name: iou
        include_background: false
      # Measured on the reassembled image by `evaluate_cases()`, not per tile.
      - name: cldice
        iterations: 12
        include_background: false
    optimizer:
      name: adam
      learning_rate: 0.001
    callbacks:
      - name: early_stopping
        monitor: val_dice
        patience: 8
        restore_best: true
    augmentation:
      - name: HorizontalFlip
        params:
          p: 0.5
      - name: VerticalFlip
        params:
          p: 0.5
seed: 1
```

Two things about that worth saying out loud.

`cldice` sits among the metrics even though the run is tiled, and the engine reassembles each
case before measuring it. **It will not appear in the epoch log**, and that is deliberate
rather than an omission: an epoch averages its metrics over batches, which is exact for Dice -
a ratio of sums - and meaningless for a skeleton, because a tile severs every vessel crossing
its edge. So there is no `val_cldice` to watch, `early_stopping` watches `val_dice`, and a
callback that asked for the other is refused when the specification is read.

`iterations: 12` is the skeleton's peel count, and it is chosen against the nine pixels
measured above: a structure nine pixels across needs about half that many erosions to reach
its centreline, and twelve leaves room for the widest vessels in the set rather than the
average one.

## Training

```python
import pyplatypus as pp

spec = pp.from_yaml("fives.yaml")
engine = pp.build_engine(spec, num_workers=4)
history = engine.fit(verbose=True)["vessels"]
```

`num_workers=4` is worth a line of its own here rather than in a footnote. Training shuffles
in windows so that one decoded image serves all sixteen of its tiles; four workers decoding
2048-pixel PNGs ahead of the GPU is the difference between an epoch that waits on the disk and
one that does not. This run took **403 minutes over 40 epochs**, with its best validation Dice
at epoch 34 - it did not stop early, which is worth remembering when the last section compares
budgets.

## One number hides the finding

```python
for row in engine.evaluate():
    print(row)
```

That is the whole test set as one row, and it is the least informative view of it. The
distribution is the finding, and `evaluate_cases()` gives it - one row per case, with clDice
measured on the reassembled image inside the same walk over the split:

```python
cases = engine.evaluate_cases("vessels")
```

Over the 200 test images: **mean Dice 0.8828, mean IoU 0.8014, mean clDice 0.8869**, best case
0.9596 and worst 0.1098. Now by the disease in the file name:

| disease | n | dice | sd | worst |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AMD | 50 | 0.9105 | 0.0474 | 0.7001 |
| diabetic retinopathy | 50 | 0.8792 | 0.0697 | 0.5807 |
| glaucoma | 50 | 0.8393 | 0.1770 | 0.1098 |
| normal | 50 | 0.9020 | 0.0452 | 0.7187 |

Glaucoma is the worst group, by several points, with four times the spread of the best one and
a worst case near zero. The reading that offers itself is that the model is worse at glaucoma.

**Before concluding that, check whether it is the group whose photographs are worse.** FIVES
ships a `Quality Assessment.xlsx` grading every image for illumination and contrast, blur and
low contrast. Nothing in this pipeline reads it. Joined to the per-case scores it inverts the
finding:

| | n | dice |
|---|---|---|
| graded clean | 133 | 0.9161 |
| graded poor on any flag | 67 | 0.8166 |

and, on the clean images alone, **glaucoma is the best of the four groups and the tightest**,
at 0.9325 with a standard deviation of 0.0232 against normal's 0.9138. What makes it the worst
group overall is that 28 of its 50 test photographs carry a flag, against 8 of AMD's - and 14
of the 15 low-contrast images in the whole test split are glaucoma.

That is the general lesson rather than a fact about retinas: a per-group table is worth having
precisely because it invites the question *why is this group different*, and the first answer
is rarely the right one.

## clDice beside Dice

Over the same 200 cases:

| | |
|---|---|
| correlation of dice and cldice | 0.9779 |
| mean of clDice minus Dice | +0.0041 |
| sd of that difference | 0.0219 |

Read the first two together, because they say different things. The **correlation** is high:
the two metrics rank the cases much the same way, so clDice is not finding a different set of
bad images. The **mean difference** is small and positive, which says the vessels this model
draws are about as connected as their pixel overlap suggests.

That is a property of the model rather than of the metric, and the R vignette's own run is the
evidence. At fifteen epochs instead of forty, clDice sits about five points *below* Dice there:
the model is getting the right pixels and breaking the lines. **The better-trained model closes
the gap**, so a large negative gap is not clDice being pessimistic - it is clDice measuring
what fifteen epochs had not finished learning, and Dice not noticing.

The last section finds the same column doing the same work across eleven objectives, which is
the strongest version of this point available.

## The worst case, drawn

A table says a case scored near zero. A picture says why.

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/maju116/pyplatypus/main/assets/article-fives-worst.png)

The top row is the first case in the split, `100_D` at Dice 0.935. The bottom row is the worst
case in the whole test set, `123_G` at 0.110, and **the photograph is nearly black** - which is
the quality finding above, arrived at from the other end. Look at the truth column rather than
the prediction: the annotator traced four vessels out of a tree, because four is what is
visible. The model found almost none of them.

Drawing it needs two images out of two hundred, and the whole split at 2048 x 2048 is about
6.7 GB, so the stream is read for the two it is asked for and the rest are dropped as they
arrive:

```python
wanted = {"100_D", "123_G"}
drawn = {
    case: whole
    for case, whole in engine.predict_stream("vessels", split="validation")
    if case in wanted
}
```

`predict_stream()` keeps one answer at a time; `predict()` would hand back all 200 at full
resolution in order to draw two of them. It is cheap in memory and not in time - the stream is
sequential, so two cases out of two hundred still run the model over two hundred.

## Two of those choices, measured afterwards

`loss: cce_dice` and `splits: [4, 4]` are the two decisions in the configuration above that
read as taste. Both have since been measured on this dataset - after this page's walk was
written, and with every arm kept rather than described - and one of the answers contradicts
the section this page opens with.

The tables below are **transcriptions**. The runs live in the project's workbench under
`measurements/fives/`, and each table is printed by a script that reads the stored records
back: `losses-read.py`, `boundary-read.py` and `tiling-read.py`. Nothing on this page runs
them.

**The setting is not this page's**, which is the first thing to know before comparing anything
to the numbers above. Every arm trained on **148 of the 600 training retinas** - every second
one within each disease group, so the four stay balanced - for up to 40 epochs with early
stopping on `val_dice` at patience 8, and every arm was scored case by case on the same 200
test images. So no absolute Dice below is comparable to the 0.8828 above; what the tables are
for is the differences, each paired case against case.

A difference is read against a measured **floor** rather than against zero. The baseline ran
twice with different seeds, and the floor is the larger of that pair's mean difference and that
mean's own standard error: **0.0009** over all 200 cases and **0.0022** over the 67 that
FIVES's quality assessment flags. The `x` columns are multiples of that floor, and a row at 2x
says nothing.

### The loss is a decision, and this configuration already had the right one

All eleven of the engine's semantic losses, at that setting:

| loss | dice | clDice - dice | vs `cce_dice` | x | flagged | x | seeds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `focal` | 0.8673 | +0.0078 | +0.0001 | 0.1 | +0.0020 | 0.9 | 1 |
| `cce` | 0.8672 | +0.0084 | +0.0000 | 0.0 | -0.0028 | 1.3 | 1 |
| `cce_dice`, the baseline | 0.8672 | +0.0052 | - | - | - | - | 2 |
| `combo` | 0.8612 | +0.0048 | -0.0060 | 6.9 | -0.0021 | 1.0 | 1 |
| `lovasz` | 0.8562 | +0.0041 | -0.0110 | 12.6 | -0.0192 | 8.7 | 2 |
| `generalized_dice` | 0.8504 | +0.0082 | -0.0167 | 19.2 | -0.0229 | 10.4 | 1 |
| `boundary`, surface 0.1 | 0.8491 | +0.0045 | -0.0181 | 20.8 | -0.0329 | 15.0 | 1 |
| `iou` | 0.8309 | +0.0098 | -0.0362 | 41.5 | -0.0482 | 21.9 | 1 |
| `boundary`, surface 0.3 | 0.8245 | -0.0051 | -0.0427 | 48.9 | -0.0581 | 26.5 | 2 |
| `tversky`, alpha 0.7 | 0.8201 | +0.0134 | -0.0471 | 53.9 | -0.0638 | 29.1 | 1 |
| `dice` | 0.8127 | +0.0154 | -0.0545 | 62.3 | -0.0648 | 29.5 | 1 |
| `focal_tversky`, 0.7 and 1.33 | 0.7913 | +0.0188 | -0.0759 | 86.9 | -0.0940 | 42.8 | 1 |

**The menu spans 0.0760 of Dice**, 87 times the floor and 25 times the 0.0030 that separated
the four architectures measured on nuclei. So the loss is a decision where the architecture
was a menu - which is worth knowing before spending an afternoon choosing between `u_net` and
`linknet`.

**And nothing in the menu beats the default.** `focal` at +0.0001 and `cce` at +0.0000 tie
`cce_dice`, both below every floor measured anywhere here, and nine rows are worse. The family
designed for thin structures under class imbalance - Tversky, Focal-Tversky, Lovasz - holds
four of the five worst rows. `cce_dice` has been this example's objective since it was written
and nobody had measured whether that was right.

Two cautions the table carries about itself:

**Nine of eleven rows have one seed.** The four at the top move by less than the seed floors
measured on any non-baseline loss here - 0.0120 for `boundary` at surface 0.3, 0.0465 for
`lovasz` - so one seed cannot distinguish them from the baseline. Everything from `boundary`
at surface 0.1 downwards is 10x to 87x the floor, and a second seed will not move it.
`lovasz` is the warning worth reading twice: one of its seeds scores 0.8706, the highest
single number in this table, and the other scores 0.8418.

**The stopping rule is a confound, and it was priced rather than argued.** Four arms stopped
early enough that part of their deficit is convergence - `focal_tversky` at 20 epochs,
`lovasz`'s second seed at 21, `dice` at 25, `iou` at 26 - while all three `boundary` arms ran
into the 40-epoch cap. Re-read at 20 epochs, the budget every arm was granted, **the ordering
does not change.**

The `clDice - dice` column also goes somewhere, and it was nobody's question: it grows as the
loss gets worse, from +0.0052 at the baseline through +0.0098 for `iou` and +0.0154 for `dice`
to +0.0188 for `focal_tversky`. A worse objective loses more Dice than clDice, so what degrades
first is the vessel's bulk and its connectedness survives longer. There is exactly one
exception, and it is the next table's subject.

### A surface loss is the one that breaks the lines, and it gets worse with the dose

`boundary` is the obvious thing to reach for on a nine-pixel structure: the boundary *is* the
object, so an objective weighing the surface should be the one that helps. It does the opposite
here, and it does so by a dose. `alpha` weights the **region** term, so the surface term's
share is `1 - alpha`:

| surface share | seeds | flagged dice vs baseline | x | clDice - dice | its own pair, flagged |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| none, the baseline | 2 | - | - | +0.0052 | 0.0012 |
| 0.1, `alpha: 0.9` | 1 | -0.0329 | 15.0 | +0.0045 | unmeasured |
| 0.3, `alpha: 0.7` | 2 | -0.0581 | 26.5 | -0.0051 | 0.0120 |

**Three times the surface term costs 1.77 times the Dice and 4.18 times the gap**, and the gap
changes sign: at surface 0.3 clDice falls below Dice, which no baseline run does. So the
argument for this loss was backwards - connectedness is what it costs first, and on the flagged
photographs it costs 15 to 27 times the noise.

Two things keep that honest. **The dose has its own noise and it is ten times the
baseline's**, which is the last column: the two arms at surface 0.3 sit 0.0120 apart on the
flagged cases where the baseline's two sit 0.0012 apart. (That column is each pair's own mean
difference; the `x` column's denominator is still the baseline's 0.0022 from above, so the two
are not the same quantity and the table would mislead if they were read as one.) That is this loss's documented behaviour - it grows noisier the more of the
objective the surface term owns - reproduced on real data, and it is also the denominator the
dose claim has to clear. Judged against it the two doses are 2.1x apart, not the twentyfold the
baseline's floor would suggest. And **both arms at the higher dose stopped on the epoch cap
with their best at the last epoch**, so part of their deficit is being undertrained rather than
being worse.

### Tiling against resizing, where this page's first section is too strong

Same data, same model, same loss. One arm tiles 2048 into 4 x 4 as the configuration above
does; two resize the whole retina to 512 and leave `splits` unset. All three are scored on the
**source grid**, 2048 x 2048, which for the resized arms means a second scoring pass.

| arm | dice | vs tiled | x | clean, 133 | flagged, 67 | clDice - dice | training |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| tiled, 4 x 4 at 2048 | 0.8672 | - | - | 0.9079 | 0.7865 | +0.0052 | 418 min |
| resized to 512, same cap | 0.8667 | -0.0005 | 0.6 | 0.8935 | 0.8134 | +0.0138 | 26 min |
| resized to 512, matched steps | 0.8705 | +0.0033 | 3.8 | 0.8984 | 0.8152 | +0.0141 | 165 min |

There are two resized arms because sixteen tiles make "the same number of epochs" the wrong
comparison: 148 retinas at `batch_size: 4` are 37 gradient steps an epoch resized and 592
tiled. The first resized arm is the comparison somebody would actually run - the same 40-epoch
cap and the same patience. The second was granted the tiled arm's 23,680 steps and **did not
spend them**, stopping on patience at 41% of the budget, so that row is converged against
converged. The truncation the first arm suffered is worth +0.0038, which is worth knowing
before budgeting for the matched arm: a measurement that cannot afford it loses 0.004 and the
ability to say so.

**The overall column says the two methods are equivalent, and it is hiding the largest effect
in the measurement.** Resizing is better by 0.027 to 0.029 on the 67 flagged photographs and
worse by 0.010 to 0.014 on the 133 clean ones, both many times their own floors - 0.0019 to
0.0025 flagged, 0.0007 to 0.0013 clean. The two are good at different pictures, and a swing of
about 0.03 in each direction averages out to 0.0033.

So what survives from "Why a vessel cannot be resized" is the narrow claim: on a clean
photograph resizing costs Dice, and `splits` is what lets an image too large to resize be
trained at all. What does not survive is the stronger reading - that resizing a 2048 retina
destroys the thin vessels - because on the hard pictures the vessels it was supposed to have
destroyed are found *more* reliably from a whole blurred eye than from a sixteenth of one. A
mechanism suggests itself and is recorded as a hypothesis rather than a finding: a 512 tile
sees one sixteenth of a retina and has no global context to tell a vessel from an artefact,
where a resized image always shows the whole eye. Separating that would need overlapping tiles
or a resized arm at 1024, and neither was run.

What tiling costs is also not what the table makes it look like. Per gradient step the three
arms are identical to within the noise of six readings, 0.502 to 0.554 s, so tiling is sixteen
times the work rather than sixteen times the overhead, and the whole factor shows up in the
epoch rather than anywhere surprising.

### The rig, which is worth more than the ranking

This is the part to carry away from all three tables, and it is about measuring rather than
about retinas.

`evaluate_cases()` builds its dataset from the model's own specification, so it scores each
model at that model's own `load_shape`. Put a tiled model beside a resized one and the first is
scored on 2048 while the second is scored on 512, against a truth reduced the same way. Nobody
passes a flag for this and nothing warns:

| arm | honest, both on 2048 | as the default comparison reports it | the rig |
|---|---|---|---|
| resized to 512, same cap | -0.0005 | +0.0056 | +0.0062 |
| resized to 512, matched steps | +0.0033 | +0.0187 | +0.0154 |

The reported figure is **5.7 times** the honest one and the rig alone is **4.7 times** the
effect. A table built that way would have concluded that resizing beats native-resolution
tiling by a wide margin, and every number in it would have been a real Dice of a real
prediction against a real mask - just not the mask the other arm was judged against.

**And the bias has the opposite sign on clDice:** +0.0096 to +0.0156 on Dice against -0.0156 to
-0.0230 on clDice. Upsampling a 512 prediction to 2048 smooths it, and a smoothed vessel agrees
better with a skeleton and worse with a boundary. So the rigged comparison flatters resizing on
Dice and penalises it on clDice, and a comparison reporting only one of the two is wrong in a
direction set by which one it picked.

**There is an option for this since `0.8.0a32`, and there was none when this was measured.**
The arms above were rescored onto one grid by a function written for that measurement, which
lived in the workbench and not in the package - so the honest comparison was available only to
somebody who had already noticed the problem, which is what `maju116/rplatypus#187` was filed
about. `evaluate(at="source")` is that function now: every prediction goes back onto the grid
of the file it came from and is scored against the truth as stored, and the `load_shape` column
reads `source` so a table says which grid produced it.

The grid is the files' own rather than one you name, and that is the point rather than a
limitation: a named grid resamples the **truth**, so the thing both models are judged against
would itself be an interpolation somebody chose. Here only predictions move.

The rule the numbers above teach is unchanged and is now enforceable rather than advisory:
**compare two models only where their predictions and the truth are on the same grid**, and say
which grid that is.

### What none of this says

One dataset, one architecture, one loss, at one reduction of one resolution, with 148 retinas
rather than 600. The subsets already disagree by about 0.03 in either direction *inside* this
dataset, which is the strongest available warning against reading any overall column as a rule.
And the published `fives-unet` weights' own score is not comparable to any row above either -
different data, a full training set, and a pinned commit.

## Notes

**The data's licence travels.** FIVES is CC BY 4.0, which is why the published `fives-unet`
weights are CC BY 4.0 rather than MIT and why their sidecar carries the citation: Jin et al.,
*FIVES: A Fundus Image Dataset for Artificial Intelligence based Vessel Segmentation*,
Scientific Data 9, 475 (2022).

**The cost.** 40 epochs over 600 retinas at 2048, cut sixteen ways, is 403 minutes on a GTX
1070; scoring the 200 test images, including reassembling each one for clDice, is about two
minutes. Tiling is what makes the first number bearable rather than worse: a tiled run reuses
each decoded image for all sixteen of its tiles, which is worth roughly a factor of two
against decoding one per tile.

**A card that uses the GPU it has.** A Pascal-generation card needs the last PyTorch built
against CUDA 12; the R package has `platypus_use_torch("pascal")` for that because it builds
its own environment, and here it is an ordinary install of a matching wheel.
